tool.name: Angular
tool.tagline: Batteries-included TypeScript framework with signals and standalone components
tool.description: Angular is a complete, opinionated framework from Google for building web applications in TypeScript, with routing, forms, HTTP, testing and server rendering built in. Modern Angular is built on standalone components, signals for fine-grained reactivity and a new template control flow, and runs zoneless by default. It is popular for large enterprise apps where consistency and long-term structure matter.

concepts.name: The Angular CLI and project structure
concepts.summary: Create, serve and build an app with the Angular CLI, and know what the generated files do.
concepts.why: The CLI is how every Angular project is created, run, generated, tested and built.
concepts.body:
Angular is used through its **CLI**. Install it with `npm install -g @angular/cli`, then:

- `ng new my-app` scaffolds a project (it asks about styles and server-side rendering).
- `ng serve` runs a dev server with hot reload at `http://localhost:4200`.
- `ng generate component user-card` (short: `ng g c user-card`) creates a component; also `service`, `directive`, `pipe`, `guard`, `interceptor`.
- `ng test` runs unit tests (Vitest by default in new projects), `ng build` produces an optimised production bundle in `dist/`.

A new project contains:

- `src/main.ts` — calls `bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig)` to start the app with the root component.
- `src/app/app.config.ts` — application-wide **providers**: the router, error listeners, HTTP features and so on.
- `src/app/app.ts`, `app.html`, `app.css` — the root component. Current style drops the `.component` suffix from file names.
- `src/app/app.routes.ts` — the route table.
- `angular.json` — build and serve configuration; `tsconfig.json` — TypeScript settings, with strict mode on.

Modern Angular (v17 onwards, and the default in v22) uses **standalone components**: each component lists what it uses in its own `imports` array, so NgModules are optional and mostly legacy. New apps are also **zoneless** (no zone.js) and components use the `OnPush` change detection strategy by default; both rely on signals, which you will learn shortly.
takeaways: `ng new`, `ng serve`, `ng generate`, `ng test`, `ng build` cover the daily workflow
`main.ts` bootstraps the root component with providers from `app.config.ts`
New apps are standalone, zoneless and OnPush by default
pitfalls: Following old tutorials that create NgModules and `app.component.ts` files; modern Angular doesn't need them.

quiz.q: Where do you register application-wide providers such as the router in a new Angular app?
options: In the providers array of app.config.ts passed to bootstrapApplication
quiz.explain: Standalone apps pass an ApplicationConfig with providers to bootstrapApplication.

concepts.name: Components
concepts.summary: Define a component with @Component: selector, template, styles and imports, and use it from another component.
concepts.why: Components are the building blocks of every Angular UI.
concepts.body:
An Angular **component** is a TypeScript class decorated with `@Component`. The decorator's metadata tells Angular how to render it: - `selector` — the custom HTML tag that places the component, e.g. `'app-user-card'` used as ``. Prefix selectors (`app-`) to avoid clashing with real HTML elements. - `template` (inline) or `templateUrl` (separate `.html` file) — the markup. - `styles` or `styleUrl` — CSS that is **encapsulated**: Angular rewrites selectors so they only match this component's elements. - `imports` — the other components, directives and pipes this template uses. If you use `` without importing `Avatar`, the build fails with an "unknown element" error. Class fields and methods are available to the template. Fields used in templates are usually `protected` (visible to the template but not part of the public API) and often signals, which you read by calling them: `{{ name() }}`. ```ts @Component({ selector: 'app-hello', template: `

Hello {{ name() }}

` }) export class Hello { protected name = signal('Ada'); } ``` Components form a tree starting at the root component bootstrapped in `main.ts`. Keep components small and focused: a page component composes smaller presentational components, each with a clear set of inputs and outputs.
takeaways: `@Component` = selector + template + styles + imports on a TypeScript class
List every component, directive and pipe the template uses in `imports`
Styles are encapsulated per component by default
pitfalls: Forgetting to add a child component to `imports`, causing "is not a known element" build errors.

quiz.q: A template uses <app-chart> but the build reports "'app-chart' is not a known element". What is the most likely fix?
options: Add the Chart component class to this component's imports array
quiz.explain: Standalone components must import every component their template uses.

concepts.name: Template bindings
concepts.summary: Show data with interpolation and bind DOM properties, attributes, classes and styles with square brackets.
concepts.why: Bindings are how component state reaches the DOM; mixing up properties and attributes is a classic Angular bug.
concepts.body:
Angular templates are HTML plus bindings that Angular keeps in sync with component state.

**Interpolation** `{{ expression }}` renders text. Expressions are a TypeScript-like subset: property access, method calls, operators, template literals, `?.` and `??`. They can't contain assignments, `new` or statements, and should be cheap and side-effect free because they are re-evaluated during change detection.

**Property binding** uses square brackets: `[disabled]="isSaving()"`, `[src]="avatarUrl()"`, `[value]="name()"`. It sets a **DOM property** (or a component input) to the evaluated value, keeping its type: booleans stay booleans. Without brackets, `disabled="false"` sets the attribute to the string "false", which still disables the button.

Some things are attributes, not properties (ARIA, `colspan`, SVG attributes, `data-*`). Bind them with **`[attr.name]`**: `[attr.aria-label]="label()"`. A `null` value removes the attribute.

**Class and style bindings**:

- `[class.active]="isActive()"` toggles one class; `[class]="{ active: a(), disabled: d() }"` takes an object, array or string.
- `[style.width.px]="width()"` sets one style with a unit; `[style]="{ color: c() }"` takes an object.

Angular sanitises values bound to `innerHTML`, URLs and styles to prevent cross-site scripting. You can declare template-local variables with **`@let`**: `@let total = price() * qty();`.
takeaways: `{{ }}` renders text; `[prop]="expr"` binds DOM properties and inputs with real types
Use `[attr.x]` for attributes such as ARIA and colspan
`[class.x]`, `[style.prop.unit]` and object forms handle classes and styles
pitfalls: Writing `disabled="{{ isDisabled }}"` or `disabled="false"`; use `[disabled]="isDisabled()"`.

quiz.q: Which binding correctly sets an ARIA attribute from component state?
quiz.explain: aria-label is an attribute without a matching DOM property, so it needs the attr. prefix.

concepts.name: Event binding
concepts.summary: Respond to user actions with (event) bindings, read $event, and use key event filters.
concepts.why: Every interactive feature starts with an event handler.
concepts.body:
**Event binding** uses parentheses: `(click)="save()"`. When the event fires, Angular evaluates the statement, usually a method call on the component.

- Pass the native event with **`$event`**: `(input)="onInput($event)"`. Type it in the method and read the target: `(event.target as HTMLInputElement).value`.
- Statements can be simple assignments or calls: `(click)="count.set(count() + 1)"`. Keep logic in methods; templates should stay declarative.
- **Key filters**: `(keyup.enter)="send()"`, `(keydown.escape)="close()"`, combinations like `(keydown.control.s)="save($event)"`.
- Any DOM event works, including custom events dispatched by web components, and component outputs use the same syntax.
- Global targets: `(window:resize)` and `(document:keydown)` are available through the component's `host` metadata, for example `host: { '(window:resize)': 'onResize()' }`.

Call `event.preventDefault()` in your handler to stop default behaviour like following a link.

In zoneless apps, a template event handler is one of the things that tells Angular to run change detection, so updating a plain field inside it still refreshes the view. Updating state from timers or promises should go through signals, which notify Angular themselves. Making all template state signals is the simplest rule.
takeaways: `(event)="handler($event)"` binds DOM events and component outputs
Key filters like `(keyup.enter)` avoid manual key checks
Keep template statements to a single method call
pitfalls: Forgetting to call the method: `(click)="save"` does nothing; write `(click)="save()"`.

quiz.q: What is $event in (input)="onInput($event)" on an <input>?
quiz.explain: For DOM events $event is the native event object; read the value from its target.

concepts.name: Control flow: @if, @for, @switch
concepts.summary: Render conditionally and repeat elements with the built-in @if, @for (with track) and @switch blocks.
concepts.why: Every list and conditional in an Angular template uses these blocks; track decides list performance.
takeaways: `@if (cond; as x) {} @else {}`, `@switch` / `@case` / `@default`
`@for (x of list; track x.id) {} @empty {}`: track is mandatory
Use `$index`, `$first`, `$last` etc. via `let`
pitfalls: Tracking by `$index` (or the object itself when data is refetched) in dynamic lists, causing every row to be recreated.

quiz.q: Why does @for require a track expression?
options: So Angular can identify items across changes and reuse or move their DOM nodes
quiz.explain: Tracking by a stable id lets Angular match items between renders instead of destroying and recreating DOM.

concepts.name: Signals: signal and computed
concepts.summary: Hold state in signals, update it with set and update, and derive values with computed.
concepts.why: Signals are the foundation of modern Angular reactivity and change detection.
concepts.body:
A **signal** is a wrapper around a value that notifies interested consumers when it changes.

```ts
count = signal(0);        // WritableSignal<number>
count();                  // read: call it like a function
count.set(5);             // replace the value
count.update((c) => c + 1);   // compute from the previous value
```

**`computed`** creates a read-only signal derived from others:

```ts
double = computed(() => this.count() * 2);
```

Computed signals are **lazy and memoised**: the function runs only when the value is read after one of its dependencies changed. Dependencies are tracked automatically from the signals read during the last run, so conditional branches create dynamic dependencies.

When a template reads a signal, Angular knows exactly which component to refresh when it changes. That is what makes zoneless, OnPush-by-default Angular work.

Rules that prevent bugs:

- **Don't mutate values in place.** `this.items().push(x)` changes the array without notifying anyone. Use `update` with a new array or object: `items.update((list) => [...list, x])`.
- Signals compare with `Object.is` by default; setting an equal value does nothing. Pass a custom `equal` option if needed.
- Keep computed functions pure: no setting other signals and no side effects inside them.
- Expose read-only views with `asReadonly()` so only the owner can write.
takeaways: Read a signal by calling it; write with `set` or `update`
`computed` is lazy, memoised and tracks dependencies automatically
Update arrays and objects immutably; in-place mutation notifies nobody
pitfalls: Mutating an array or object inside a signal and expecting the UI to update.

quiz.q: `items = signal([1, 2])`, then `items().push(3)`. A template shows items().length. What does it show?
options: 2, because the signal never learned about the change
quiz.explain: push mutates the array without calling set/update, so the signal doesn't notify consumers.

concepts.name: Inputs and outputs
concepts.summary: Pass data into components with input() and send events out with output().
concepts.why: Inputs and outputs define a component's public API and how parents and children communicate.
concepts.body:
Components receive data through **inputs** and notify parents through **outputs**.

**Inputs** are declared with the `input()` function, which returns a read-only signal:

```ts
name = input.required<string>();     // parent must provide it
size = input(48);                    // optional with default
disabled = input(false, { transform: booleanAttribute });
```

The parent binds with brackets, `<app-avatar [name]="user().name" [size]="64" />`, or as a static string for strings. Because inputs are signals, you can derive from them with `computed(() => this.size() * 2)`. Required inputs can't be read before Angular sets them, so don't read them in the constructor; read them in templates, computeds or lifecycle hooks. Transforms like `booleanAttribute` let `<app-x disabled />` work as `true`.

**Outputs** are declared with `output()`:

```ts
selected = output<User>();
this.selected.emit(user);
```

The parent listens with event syntax: `(selected)="onSelect($event)"`, where `$event` is the emitted value. Output events don't bubble through the DOM.

Use `alias` options sparingly, keep inputs immutable (the child never writes to them; `input()` signals have no `set`), and name outputs after what happened (`selected`, `closed`), not after what the parent should do. Older code uses `@Input()` and `@Output()` decorators with `EventEmitter`; they still work.
takeaways: `input()` / `input.required<T>()` declare inputs as read-only signals
`output<T>()` declares events; `emit(value)` sends them, parents get `$event`
Don't read required inputs in the constructor
pitfalls: Reading a required input in the constructor, which throws because it hasn't been set yet.

quiz.q: A child declares `closed = output<string>()` and calls this.closed.emit('esc'). How does the parent receive 'esc'?
quiz.explain: Outputs are bound with event syntax; $event holds the emitted value.

concepts.name: Services and dependency injection
concepts.summary: Put shared logic and state in services and get them anywhere with inject().
concepts.why: Dependency injection is how Angular apps share state, call APIs and stay testable.
takeaways: Services hold shared logic and state; components inject them
`@Service()` (v22) or `@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })` makes an app-wide singleton
Call `inject()` only in an injection context such as field initializers
pitfalls: Calling `inject()` inside an event handler or `setTimeout`, outside an injection context.

quiz.q: Two unrelated components both call inject(CartStore), which is provided in root. What do they get?
options: Copies that sync on change detection
quiz.explain: A root-provided service is created once and shared by every injector below the root.

concepts.name: Pipes
concepts.summary: Format values in templates with built-in pipes like date, currency and json, and write a custom pure pipe.
concepts.why: Pipes keep formatting out of components and are reused across the whole app.
concepts.body:
A **pipe** transforms a value for display: `{{ value | pipeName:arg1:arg2 }}`. Pipes can be chained, left to right.

Common built-in pipes from `@angular/common` (import them in the component's `imports`, or import `CommonModule`):

- `date`: `{{ createdAt | date:'mediumDate' }}` or a format like `'yyyy-MM-dd'`.
- `currency`, `number` (`'1.0-2'` = min 1 integer digit, 0 to 2 decimals), `percent`.
- `uppercase`, `lowercase`, `titlecase`, `slice`, `keyvalue`.
- `json` for debugging objects.
- `async` subscribes to an Observable or Promise and renders the latest value, unsubscribing automatically.

Formatting uses the app's locale (`LOCALE_ID`), so dates and currencies localise correctly.

A **custom pipe** is a class with `@Pipe({ name })` implementing `transform(value, ...args)`. Pipes are **pure** by default: Angular calls `transform` again only when the input value or arguments change by reference. That makes them cheap, but it also means mutating an array in place won't re-run a pure pipe. Impure pipes (`pure: false`) run on every change detection and should be avoided for anything expensive.

Pipes are better than calling a method in the template for formatting, since methods run on every change detection pass. For component-specific derived data, a `computed` signal is usually clearer.
takeaways: `{{ value | pipe:arg }}` formats values; chain pipes left to right
Import pipes like `DatePipe` and `CurrencyPipe` into the component
Custom pipes are pure by default and only re-run when inputs change by reference
pitfalls: Mutating an array in place and expecting a pure pipe that filters it to update.

quiz.q: A pure custom pipe filters an array. You push a new item into the same array. Does the displayed result change?
options: No, the array reference didn't change so the pure pipe isn't re-run
Only if the pipe is in imports
quiz.explain: Pure pipes re-run only when the input reference or arguments change.

concepts.name: effect, linkedSignal and untracked
concepts.summary: Run side effects when signals change, create writable state that resets from a source, and read signals without tracking.
concepts.why: Real apps must sync signals with storage, logging and third-party code, and keep dependent state consistent.
takeaways: `effect` is for side effects outside signals; create it in an injection context
`linkedSignal` = writable state that resets when its source changes
`untracked` reads a signal without creating a dependency
pitfalls: Using an effect to set one signal from another; that causes extra cycles and glitches. Use computed or linkedSignal.

quiz.q: A list of options can change, and the selection should reset to the first option when it does, while users can still pick another. What fits best?
quiz.explain: linkedSignal is writable like a signal but recomputes from its source whenever the source changes.

concepts.name: Two-way binding with model()
concepts.summary: Build components that support [(value)] two-way binding with model() signals.
concepts.why: Custom inputs, toggles and pickers should be as easy to bind as native form controls.
concepts.body:
**Two-way binding** combines a property binding and an event binding: `[(value)]="x"` is shorthand for `[value]="x" (valueChange)="x = $event"` (the "banana in a box" syntax).

The **`model()`** function creates both sides in one declaration:

```ts
checked = model(false);          // ModelSignal<boolean>
this.checked.set(true);          // updates locally AND emits checkedChange
```

A model is a writable signal inside the child. When the child calls `set` or `update`, Angular emits `checkedChange` and the parent's bound value updates. When the parent's value changes, the model receives it like an input.

In the parent, bind a **writable signal** directly: `<app-toggle [(checked)]="darkMode" />` where `darkMode = signal(false)`. Angular reads and writes the signal for you (note: no parentheses after `darkMode`). Binding a plain field also works.

`model.required<T>()` makes the binding mandatory. A model can also be used one-way: the parent can just pass `[checked]="x"` or just listen with `(checkedChange)`.

Use `model()` for value-like components (rating, toggle, date picker, tabs' active index). For components that should integrate with Angular forms (validation, touched state), signal forms let custom controls implement a small interface built on `model()` too.
takeaways: `model()` declares a writable, two-way bindable signal input
Bind a writable signal directly: `[(value)]="score"` without calling it
pitfalls: Writing `[(value)]="score()"` with parentheses; two-way binding needs the signal itself, not its value.

quiz.q: Inside a child, `open = model(false)` and the code calls this.open.set(true). What happens?
options: Angular throws because models are read-only
The child's value changes and openChange is emitted so a two-way bound parent updates
quiz.explain: Setting a model signal updates it and emits the matching Change event.

concepts.name: Content projection and queries
concepts.summary: Pass markup into components with ng-content and reach child elements and components with viewChild and contentChild.
concepts.why: Layout components (cards, dialogs, tabs) depend on projection, and integrations need direct element access.
concepts.body:
**Content projection** lets a parent pass markup into a child. The child marks where it goes with ``: ```html

Any content

 ``` Multiple slots use `select` with a CSS selector: `` receives elements with that attribute, and a plain `` takes the rest. A fallback can be placed inside `` itself. Projected content is created by the parent and belongs to the parent's scope; the child can't conditionally create or re-create it. For lazily rendered or repeated content, pass an `` and render it with `ngTemplateOutlet`. **Queries** give a component references to things in its template or projected content, as signals: - `viewChild('ref')` finds an element or component with a template reference variable `#ref` in its own template; `viewChild(ChildComponent)` finds by type. The result is an `ElementRef` for elements. - `viewChild.required(...)` when it always exists; `viewChildren(...)` for all matches. - `contentChild(...)` and `contentChildren(...)` search **projected** content, e.g. a tabs component finding its `` children. Query signals are `undefined` until the view is created, so read them in `computed`, `effect`, `afterNextRender` or event handlers rather than the constructor.
takeaways: `<ng-content />` projects parent markup; `select` creates named slots
`viewChild`/`viewChildren` query the component's own template
`contentChild`/`contentChildren` query projected content; results are signals
pitfalls: Reading a view query in the constructor, before the view exists.

quiz.q: A Tabs component needs the list of <app-tab> elements the parent placed between its tags. Which query fits?
quiz.explain: Projected content is queried with content queries; view queries only see the component's own template.

concepts.name: Lifecycle hooks, DestroyRef and render hooks
concepts.summary: Run code at the right moment: ngOnInit, ngOnChanges, ngOnDestroy, DestroyRef, afterNextRender and afterRenderEffect.
concepts.why: Initialising data, cleaning up subscriptions and touching the DOM safely all depend on lifecycle timing.
concepts.body:
Angular calls **lifecycle hooks** on components and directives as they are created, updated and destroyed. Implement them as methods (with the matching interface for type safety):

- `ngOnInit()` — once, after the first inputs are set. Classic place to start loading data based on inputs.
- `ngOnChanges(changes)` — whenever decorator-based inputs change. With signal inputs you rarely need it: use `computed` or `effect`.
- `ngOnDestroy()` — before the component is removed; clean up timers and subscriptions.
- `ngAfterViewInit()` and `ngAfterContentInit()` — after the view or projected content is first created.

**`DestroyRef`** is the composable alternative to `ngOnDestroy`: `inject(DestroyRef).onDestroy(() => ...)` works in services, directives and helper functions, which is how utilities like `takeUntilDestroyed` clean up automatically.

For DOM work, use the **render hooks**:

- `afterNextRender(fn)` runs once after the next render, in the browser only. Use it to initialise charts, measure elements or focus inputs.
- `afterRenderEffect(fn)` runs after rendering whenever signals it reads change.
- `afterEveryRender(fn)` runs after every render (use sparingly).

Render hooks never run during server-side rendering, so they are the safe place for browser APIs. All of these registration functions must be called in an injection context, typically the constructor.
takeaways: `ngOnInit` after first inputs; `ngOnDestroy` or `DestroyRef.onDestroy` for cleanup
With signal inputs prefer `computed`/`effect` over `ngOnChanges`
`afterNextRender` / `afterRenderEffect` for browser-only DOM work
pitfalls: Touching `window` or the DOM in the constructor or ngOnInit of an SSR app; use render hooks.

quiz.q: Where should you initialise a third-party chart library that needs the canvas element, in an app that also renders on the server?
quiz.explain: afterNextRender runs after the DOM is rendered and only in the browser.

concepts.name: Routing
concepts.summary: Configure routes, render them with router-outlet, link with routerLink, lazy-load components and read params as inputs.
concepts.why: Every multi-page Angular app is built around the router.
concepts.body:
The Angular **router** maps URLs to components. Define a `Routes` array and register it with `provideRouter(routes)` in `app.config.ts`:

```ts
export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', component: Home, title: 'Home' },
  { path: 'products/:id', loadComponent: () => import('./product/product').then((m) => m.ProductPage) },
  { path: '**', component: NotFound },
];
```

- The root template contains `<router-outlet />` (import `RouterOutlet`), where the matched component renders.
- **Lazy loading** with `loadComponent` (one component) or `loadChildren` (a child route array) splits the bundle so code loads on demand.
- `children` define nested routes rendered in a nested outlet; `redirectTo` with `pathMatch: 'full'` redirects; `'**'` catches everything else (put it last; routes match in order).
- `title` sets the document title.

**Navigation**: `<a routerLink="/products/42">` or `[routerLink]="['/products', p.id]"` (import `RouterLink`), with `routerLinkActive="active"` for styling. In code, `inject(Router).navigate(['/products', id])`.

**Reading parameters**: with `provideRouter(routes, withComponentInputBinding())`, route params, query params and resolved data are bound to component inputs of the same name: `id = input.required<string>()`. Because it is a signal, the component updates when you navigate from `/products/1` to `/products/2` (the same component instance is reused). Without input binding, inject `ActivatedRoute` and read its observables.
takeaways: Define `Routes`, `provideRouter(routes)`, render in `<router-outlet />`
Lazy-load with `loadComponent` / `loadChildren`
`withComponentInputBinding()` maps params to inputs; the component is reused across param changes
pitfalls: Placing the `'**'` wildcard route before other routes; matching is first-come, so it swallows everything.

quiz.q: Navigating from /products/1 to /products/2 shows the same component. With withComponentInputBinding and id = input.required<string>(), what happens?
options: The same instance is reused and the id() signal changes to '2'
The component is destroyed and recreated
quiz.explain: The router reuses the component when only params change; signal inputs make the change visible.

concepts.name: HttpClient and interceptors
concepts.summary: Call APIs with HttpClient, type responses, handle errors and add cross-cutting behaviour with functional interceptors.
concepts.why: Talking to a backend is central to most Angular apps, and interceptors centralise auth and error handling.
concepts.body:
**`HttpClient`** (from `@angular/common/http`) is Angular's HTTP API. It is available for injection by default and uses `fetch` under the hood. You add features with `provideHttpClient(...)` in `app.config.ts`, for example interceptors.

```ts
private http = inject(HttpClient);
getUsers() { return this.http.get<User[]>('/api/users'); }
```

Methods (`get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`) return an RxJS **Observable**. Key facts:

- Observables are **cold**: no request is sent until something subscribes (`.subscribe()`, the `async` pipe, `toSignal`, `firstValueFrom`). Each subscription sends a new request.
- The response body is parsed as JSON by default; the type parameter (`get<User[]>`) is a compile-time assertion, not validation.
- Options include `params`, `headers`, `responseType` and `observe: 'response'` for status and headers.
- Errors arrive as `HttpErrorResponse` in the error callback or `catchError`.

For most read-only data in components, prefer `httpResource` (next lesson), which wraps HttpClient in signals.

**Interceptors** are functions that see every request and response:

```ts
export const authInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) =>
  next(req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${inject(Auth).token()}` } }));
```

Register them with `provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor]))`. Requests are immutable, so use `clone`. Interceptors handle auth headers, logging, retries, error toasts and loading indicators.
takeaways: `inject(HttpClient).get<T>(url)` returns a cold Observable; nothing is sent until subscribed
The type parameter is not runtime validation
Functional interceptors (`HttpInterceptorFn`) clone and modify requests for every call
pitfalls: Calling `this.http.post(...)` without subscribing, so the request is never sent.

quiz.q: A service method returns this.http.delete('/api/items/1'), and a click handler calls it without subscribe(). What happens?
options: No request is sent because the Observable is never subscribed
quiz.explain: HttpClient observables are cold; the request is made per subscription.

concepts.name: Async data with resource and httpResource
concepts.summary: Load async data as signals with httpResource and resource: reactive params, loading and error state, reload and abort.
concepts.why: Resources are the signal-native way to fetch data in Angular, replacing hand-written loading and error flags.
concepts.body:
A **resource** turns asynchronous data into signals. It re-fetches automatically when the signals it depends on change, and it exposes state you can use in templates.

**`httpResource`** (from `@angular/common/http`) wraps HttpClient. Pass a function that returns the URL (or a request object); signals read inside it make the resource reactive:

```ts
user = httpResource<User>(() => `/api/users/${this.userId()}`);
```

**`resource`** (from `@angular/core`) works with any Promise-based loader:

```ts
weather = resource({
  params: () => ({ city: this.city() }),
  loader: ({ params, abortSignal }) => fetch(`/api/weather?city=${params.city}`, { signal: abortSignal }).then((r) => r.json()),
});
```

A resource exposes:

- `value()` — the data (`undefined` until loaded); `hasValue()` narrows it safely.
- `isLoading()`, `error()`, and `status()` (`'idle' | 'loading' | 'reloading' | 'resolved' | 'error' | 'local'`).
- `reload()` to fetch again, and `set`/`update` to change the value locally (for optimistic updates).

When params change while a request is in flight, the previous request is **aborted** (through `abortSignal`), so stale responses never win. If the params or URL function returns `undefined`, the loader doesn't run and the resource stays idle, a neat way to wait for required input.

Use resources for reading data. Mutations (POST/PUT) should be explicit calls in event handlers or form submission, followed by `reload()` if needed.
takeaways: `httpResource(() => url)` and `resource({ params, loader })` expose async data as signals
Use `value()`, `hasValue()`, `isLoading()`, `error()`, `status()` and `reload()`
Changing params aborts the in-flight request; returning undefined keeps it idle
pitfalls: Using a resource for POST/DELETE mutations; resources are for reading reactive data.

quiz.q: The URL function of an httpResource returns undefined because no user is selected yet. What happens?
options: The resource stays idle and makes no request
It retries until a value appears
quiz.explain: Returning undefined from the request/params function means there is nothing to load yet.

concepts.name: Signal forms
concepts.summary: Build typed, validated forms from a signal model with form(), schema validators and the [formField] directive.
concepts.why: Signal forms are Angular's modern forms API: less boilerplate than reactive forms and fully signal-based.
takeaways: `form(modelSignal, schemaFn)` builds a typed field tree that writes into the model
Bind inputs with `[formField]`; read state via `field().valid()`, `errors()`, `touched()`
Validators (`required`, `email`, `minLength`, `validate`...) are declared in the schema
`submit()` validates, tracks submitting and applies server errors
pitfalls: Keeping a separate copy of the data and syncing it with the form; the model signal already is the form value.

quiz.q: With signal forms, where is the current value of the whole form?
options: Only in loginForm.value property after submit
In the model signal passed to form(); the UI writes into it
quiz.explain: Signal forms use your writable signal as the source of truth, so model() always reflects user input.

concepts.name: RxJS and signals interop
concepts.summary: Bridge Observables and signals with toSignal, toObservable, takeUntilDestroyed, rxResource and outputFromObservable.
concepts.why: Much Angular code and many libraries are RxJS-based; mixing them cleanly with signals is an everyday senior skill.
concepts.body:
Signals hold a **current value**; RxJS Observables model **streams of events over time** with powerful operators (debounce, switchMap, retry, combine). Angular's `@angular/core/rxjs-interop` package bridges the two.

- **`toSignal(obs$, { initialValue })`** subscribes immediately and exposes the latest value as a signal; it unsubscribes when the component or service is destroyed. Without `initialValue` the signal is `undefined` until the first emission; `{ requireSync: true }` is for sources like `BehaviorSubject` that emit synchronously.
- **`toObservable(sig)`** turns a signal into an Observable that emits (asynchronously, via an effect) when the signal changes, so you can apply operators like `debounceTime` and `switchMap`.
- **`takeUntilDestroyed()`** completes a subscription when the current component or service is destroyed. Call it in an injection context, or pass a `DestroyRef`.
- **`rxResource({ params, stream })`** is the resource API with an Observable loader.
- **`outputFromObservable(obs$)`** exposes an Observable as a component output, and `outputToObservable` converts the other way.

A typical pattern for type-ahead search: signal for the query, `toObservable` plus `debounceTime`, `distinctUntilChanged` and `switchMap` to the API (cancelling stale requests), then `toSignal` for the template.

Rule of thumb: use signals for state shown in templates, RxJS for complex event orchestration, and convert at the boundary.
takeaways: `toSignal` reads an Observable as a signal and unsubscribes automatically
`toObservable` lets you apply RxJS operators to signal changes
`takeUntilDestroyed()` ties subscriptions to the component lifetime
pitfalls: Calling `toSignal` inside a method or event handler, creating a new subscription each time (and failing outside an injection context).

quiz.q: Why use switchMap rather than mergeMap for a type-ahead search request?
options: switchMap cancels the previous inner request when a new query arrives, so stale results can't overwrite new ones
quiz.explain: switchMap unsubscribes from the previous inner Observable, cancelling the outdated HTTP request.

concepts.name: Reactive forms
concepts.summary: Work with the established FormGroup/FormControl API: typed forms, validators, formControlName and valueChanges.
concepts.why: Most existing Angular codebases and many libraries use reactive forms, so you need to read and maintain them.
concepts.body:
Before signal forms, the standard for complex forms was **reactive forms** (`ReactiveFormsModule`). They remain fully supported and are everywhere in existing code.

The form model is a tree of control objects created in the class:

- `FormControl` holds one value plus validation state.
- `FormGroup` groups named controls; `FormArray` holds a dynamic list.
- `FormBuilder` (via `inject(FormBuilder).nonNullable`) shortens creation: `fb.group({ email: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.email]] })`.

Forms are **strictly typed** since Angular 14: `form.value.email` is `string | undefined` (disabled controls are excluded from `value`), while `form.getRawValue()` includes everything. `nonNullable` makes `reset()` return to the initial value instead of `null`.

The template binds with directives: `[formGroup]="form"` on the `<form>`, `formControlName="email"` on inputs, `formGroupName`/`formArrayName` for nesting, and `(ngSubmit)` for submission.

Validation: built-in `Validators` (`required`, `email`, `minLength`, `pattern`...), custom `ValidatorFn`s returning an error object or `null`, async validators, and group-level validators for cross-field rules. Check `control.hasError('required')`, `invalid`, `touched` and `dirty`.

Changes are exposed as Observables: `valueChanges` and `statusChanges`, often combined with RxJS or converted with `toSignal`. Custom inputs integrate by implementing `ControlValueAccessor`.
takeaways: `FormGroup`/`FormControl`/`FormArray` model the form in the class; templates bind with `formControlName`
Forms are typed; `nonNullable` makes reset restore initial values
`valueChanges`/`statusChanges` are Observables; validators return error objects or null
pitfalls: Reading `form.value` and missing disabled controls; use `getRawValue()` when you need every field.

quiz.q: A control is disabled. Is its value included in form.value?
options: No, disabled controls are excluded from value; getRawValue() includes them
quiz.explain: FormGroup.value omits disabled controls, which is also reflected in its type.

concepts.name: Attribute directives and host bindings
concepts.summary: Add reusable behaviour to elements with attribute directives, host bindings and listeners, and compose them with hostDirectives.
concepts.why: Directives package cross-cutting behaviour (tooltips, permissions, autofocus) without wrapper components.
concepts.body:
A **directive** is like a component without a template: it attaches behaviour to an existing element. **Attribute directives** are selected by an attribute, e.g. `selector: '[appHighlight]'`, and applied with `

`. Inside a directive you can: - Accept inputs with `input()`. Using the selector's name as an input alias lets you write `

`. - Inject the host element with `inject(ElementRef)` (use sparingly; prefer bindings). - Declare **host bindings and listeners** in the `host` metadata: `host: { '[class.active]': 'active()', '(mouseenter)': 'show()', 'role': 'button' }`. This is the recommended replacement for the `@HostBinding` and `@HostListener` decorators. - Inject services and other directives on the same element. Components can also use `host` to style or annotate their own host element. **`hostDirectives`** composes directives into a component or directive: `hostDirectives: [{ directive: Tooltip, inputs: ['tooltip'] }]` applies `Tooltip` to every instance and exposes its input, letting you build components from reusable behaviours without inheritance. **Structural directives** (with `*`, like the legacy `*ngIf`) create and destroy views from an ``; with built-in control flow you rarely need to write one. Remember to add directives to the `imports` of the components that use them.
takeaways: Attribute directives add behaviour via a selector like `[appX]`
Use `host: {...}` for host bindings and listeners instead of decorators
`hostDirectives` composes reusable behaviour into components
pitfalls: Manipulating the DOM directly through ElementRef when a host binding would do; it breaks SSR and bypasses sanitisation.

quiz.q:
How do you let `

` pass 'red' into a directive's color input?
quiz.explain: Aliasing an input to the selector name lets the attribute itself carry the value.

concepts.name: Route guards, resolvers and redirects
concepts.summary: Protect routes with functional guards (canActivate, canMatch, canDeactivate) and preload data with resolvers.
concepts.why: Authentication, permissions, unsaved-change prompts and data preloading are built on these router hooks.
concepts.body:
The router can run functions before activating a route. Modern guards are plain functions that can `inject()` services.

- **`canActivate`**: may the user enter this route? Return `true`, `false`, a `UrlTree` (redirect, e.g. `inject(Router).createUrlTree(['/login'])`), or a `RedirectCommand`; Promises and Observables of these work too.
- **`canMatch`**: should this route definition even be considered? If false, the router tries the next matching route, and lazy-loaded code isn't downloaded. Good for role-based alternatives (admin vs user dashboard at the same path).
- **`canActivateChild`**: guard every child route.
- **`canDeactivate`**: may the user leave? Receives the component instance, used for "unsaved changes" confirms.

**Resolvers** (`ResolveFn<T>`) fetch data before the route activates; the result is available as route data, and with component input binding as an input of the same name. Resolvers delay navigation until data arrives, so use them for small, essential data; for most pages, loading in the component with a resource gives faster perceived navigation.

Guards run on navigation, which is a UX layer only: **always enforce authorisation on the server**, since client code can be bypassed.

Keep guards small and reusable, e.g. a `roleGuard('admin')` factory that returns a `CanActivateFn`.
takeaways: Guards are functions returning boolean, UrlTree/RedirectCommand, or async versions
`canMatch` also prevents lazy code from loading; `canDeactivate` guards leaving
Resolvers preload data but delay navigation
Client guards are UX; enforce security on the server
pitfalls: Treating route guards as security; anyone can call your API directly.

quiz.q: Which guard prevents a lazy-loaded admin bundle from even being downloaded for non-admins?
quiz.explain: If canMatch returns false the route isn't matched, so its loadChildren never runs.

concepts.name: Deferrable views with @defer
concepts.summary: Lazy-load parts of a template with @defer, triggers like on viewport and on interaction, prefetching and placeholder blocks.
concepts.why: @defer cuts initial bundle size and speeds up first render with almost no code.
takeaways: `@defer (trigger) {}` splits used components into a lazy chunk
Triggers: idle (default), viewport, interaction, hover, immediate, timer, when
`prefetch on ...` downloads early; `@placeholder`, `@loading`, `@error` handle states
pitfalls: Importing a deferred component somewhere else in the same file (or using it outside the block), which makes it load eagerly.

quiz.q: A component is used inside @defer but also referenced in a ViewChild query in the same file. What happens?
options: It becomes an eager dependency, so it is not deferred
quiz.explain: Dependencies are only deferred if they aren't referenced outside the @defer block in that file.

concepts.name: Testing components and services
concepts.summary: Unit-test Angular code with TestBed and Vitest: configure providers, render components, await stability and mock HTTP.
concepts.why: Tests keep large Angular apps maintainable; TestBed is the standard way to test with real DI and templates.
concepts.body:
New Angular projects use **Vitest** as the unit test runner (older ones use Karma and Jasmine; the APIs below are the same). Run tests with `ng test`.

**TestBed** creates a testing module with Angular's DI and compiler:

- Services: `TestBed.inject(MyService)` after `TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [...] })`. Replace dependencies with fakes using `{ provide: Real, useValue: fake }`.
- Components: `const fixture = TestBed.createComponent(MyComponent)`; `fixture.componentInstance` is the class, `fixture.nativeElement` is the DOM.
- Set inputs with `fixture.componentRef.setInput('name', 'Ada')`.
- In zoneless apps, **`await fixture.whenStable()`** waits for change detection and pending work after you change state or trigger events; `fixture.detectChanges()` forces a synchronous pass.

For HTTP, provide `provideHttpClient()` and `provideHttpClientTesting()`, then use **`HttpTestingController`**: `httpMock.expectOne('/api/todos').flush([...])` returns fake data, and `httpMock.verify()` checks there were no unexpected requests.

Test behaviour as a user sees it: query the DOM, click buttons (`button.click()`), assert rendered text. **Component harnesses** (from the CDK) give a stable API for interacting with complex components like Angular Material's.

Pure logic (pipes, utility functions, computed-heavy services) can be tested as plain classes without TestBed. For end-to-end tests, use Playwright or Cypress.
takeaways: `TestBed.configureTestingModule` + `createComponent`/`inject` for tests with real DI
Use `setInput` for inputs and `await fixture.whenStable()` in zoneless apps
`provideHttpClientTesting` + `HttpTestingController` fake HTTP responses
pitfalls: Asserting on the DOM right after changing state without awaiting `whenStable()` or calling `detectChanges()`.

quiz.q: How do you set a signal input named 'user' on a component under test?
quiz.explain: Signal inputs are read-only from the class side; setInput sets them as a parent binding would.

concepts.name: Change detection: zoneless and OnPush
concepts.summary: Understand how Angular decides what to re-render: signals, OnPush (now the default), zoneless scheduling and markForCheck.
concepts.why: Change detection is the source of most Angular performance problems and the 'view didn't update' class of bugs.
concepts.body:
**Change detection** is how Angular syncs component state to the DOM: it walks component views and re-evaluates template bindings, updating the DOM where values changed.

Historically, **zone.js** patched browser async APIs and triggered a check of the whole app after every event, timer or XHR. Since Angular 21, new apps are **zoneless**: nothing is monkey-patched, and Angular schedules change detection only when it is **notified**. Notifications come from:

- a signal read in a template changing,
- a template or host event listener firing,
- `markForCheck()` (also called by the `async` pipe), `setInput`, or attaching a view.

Angular 22 also makes **`OnPush`** the default strategy (the old behaviour is now called `ChangeDetectionStrategy.Eager`). An OnPush component is checked only when it is marked dirty: its inputs changed (by reference), an event fired in it, or a signal it reads changed. Signals go further: a signal change marks only the consuming component for refresh, so Angular can skip clean ancestors.

Consequences:

- Mutating a plain field from a `setTimeout`, promise or third-party callback won't update the view. Use signals (or call `markForCheck`).
- Mutating an input object in place doesn't change its reference, so OnPush children won't refresh.
- In development, Angular runs a second check and throws **NG0100 ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked** if a binding changed during the check, which points to state updates in the wrong place.

Migrating older apps: `provideZonelessChangeDetection()` and Eager components ease the transition.
takeaways: Zoneless Angular renders only when notified: signals, template events, markForCheck
OnPush is the default in v22; components refresh when marked dirty
Prefer signals for all template state; mutate inputs immutably
NG0100 in dev reveals state changed during a check
pitfalls: Updating plain fields in timers or library callbacks and wondering why the zoneless view doesn't refresh.

quiz.q: In a zoneless app, a promise callback sets this.title = 'x' (a plain field) and nothing else happens. Does the view update?
options: Not necessarily; nothing notified Angular, so use a signal or markForCheck
quiz.explain: Without zone.js, Angular needs a notification such as a signal change to schedule rendering.

quiz.q: A parent mutates an object passed as an input to an OnPush child (obj.name = 'B'). Why might the child not update?
options: The input reference didn't change, so the child isn't marked dirty
quiz.explain: OnPush compares input references; in-place mutation keeps the same reference.

concepts.name: Hierarchical injectors and providers
concepts.summary: Master the injector tree: environment vs element injectors, provider types, InjectionToken, multi providers and resolution modifiers.
concepts.why: Scoping services correctly avoids shared-state bugs, enables per-feature configuration and powers library design.
concepts.body:
Angular has a **tree of injectors**, and `inject(Token)` walks it from the requesting point upward until a provider is found.

- **Element injectors** come from `providers` (and `viewProviders`) in `@Component`/`@Directive`. Each component instance gets its own instance of those services, shared with its descendants. Use it for state scoped to a widget, e.g. one `FormState` per wizard.
- **Environment injectors** come from `bootstrapApplication` providers (root), `@Service()`/`providedIn: 'root'`, and route-level `providers`, which create a child environment injector for that route subtree (useful for feature-scoped configuration).

Resolution checks the element injector chain first (from the requesting element up to the root component), then the environment injector chain. If nothing is found, it throws `NullInjectorError`.

**Provider forms**: `{ provide: T, useClass: Impl }`, `useValue`, `useFactory: () => ...` (factories can call `inject`), and `useExisting` (alias). **`InjectionToken<T>`** provides non-class values (config objects, functions) with a type; it can carry its own `factory` to be tree-shakable. **`multi: true`** collects several providers into an array, a plugin pattern used by things like `HTTP_INTERCEPTORS` and form validators.

Resolution modifiers via `inject(T, { optional, self, skipSelf, host })` control the search: `optional` returns `null` instead of throwing; `self` looks only at the current element; `skipSelf` starts at the parent (useful for nested tree components); `host` stops at the host component.
takeaways: Element injectors (component providers) scope instances per component subtree
Environment injectors: root, application and route-level providers
useClass/useValue/useFactory/useExisting, InjectionToken and multi providers
`inject(T, { optional, self, skipSelf, host })` controls the lookup
pitfalls: Providing a stateful service in a component's providers by accident, creating separate instances where a singleton was expected.

quiz.q: Two sibling <app-counter-panel> components each list Counter in their providers. How many Counter instances exist?
options: It throws a duplicate provider error
quiz.explain: Element-level providers create an instance per component, shared only with that component's descendants.

concepts.name: SSR, hydration and render modes
concepts.summary: Render Angular on the server, choose per-route render modes, hydrate with event replay and incremental hydration, and avoid SSR pitfalls.
concepts.why: Server rendering improves first paint and SEO, but introduces platform-specific bugs that need expert handling.
concepts.body:
Angular's SSR support lives in `@angular/ssr`. Create an app with `ng new --ssr` or add it with `ng add @angular/ssr`.

**Render modes per route** are configured in `app.routes.server.ts` with `ServerRoute` entries: `RenderMode.Prerender` (static HTML at build time, with `getPrerenderParams` for dynamic segments), `RenderMode.Server` (rendered per request) or `RenderMode.Client` (browser only). They are registered with `provideServerRendering(withRoutes(serverRoutes))` in the server config.

**Hydration** reuses the server-rendered DOM instead of re-creating it. It is enabled with `provideClientHydration()`; add `withEventReplay()` to capture clicks that happen before the code loads and replay them, and `withIncrementalHydration()` to keep parts of the page dehydrated until needed: `@defer (hydrate on viewport)` or `hydrate on interaction` renders the content on the server but only downloads and hydrates its code when triggered.

HttpClient requests made during SSR are cached into the HTML and reused on the client (the HTTP transfer cache), so data isn't fetched twice.

Pitfalls:

- No `window`, `document` layout or `localStorage` on the server. Use `afterNextRender` or check `isPlatformBrowser(inject(PLATFORM_ID))`, and inject `DOCUMENT` instead of the global.
- Hydration requires the DOM to match: direct DOM manipulation or invalid HTML nesting causes errors (`ngSkipHydration` is an escape hatch).
- Long-running timers or never-completing work keep the server waiting for the app to become stable.
- Server-side, services are per request, but module-level variables are shared between users.
takeaways: Per-route `RenderMode`: Prerender, Server or Client
`provideClientHydration()` with event replay and incremental hydration (`@defer (hydrate on ...)`)
Browser-only code goes in `afterNextRender` or behind `isPlatformBrowser`
HttpClient responses are transferred from server to client automatically
pitfalls: Reading `localStorage` during rendering, which crashes on the server or causes a hydration mismatch.

quiz.q: What does @defer (hydrate on viewport) do in an SSR app with incremental hydration?
options: Prerenders it at build time only
Renders it only in the browser after scroll
Skips rendering the block on the server
Renders it on the server, then downloads and hydrates its code when it enters the viewport
quiz.explain: Incremental hydration keeps server-rendered HTML visible and hydrates the block lazily on the trigger.
